idiom_name: Map<string, Promise<T>> with canonical keys and delete-on-settle
implementation_notes: The same idiom as JavaScript with a type discipline: the registry is Map<string, Promise<T>>, the key is a canonical string (objects compare by identity in a Map, so composite keys must be serialised), and the promise's rejection channel carries the domain error type. TypeScript adds one honest risk surface: Promise<T> is covariant in T, so a shared promise must not be widened or narrowed at call sites - the registry is the single place allowed to fix T. Everything else - the synchronous insert, the delete on settle, per-waiter races for timeouts - matches the JavaScript form.
pitfalls: Map keys compare objects by identity: build a canonical string key (or a value-keyed map) or the same logical request lands in different flights.
Typed errors are shared too: one rejection object reaches every waiter, so the error type is part of the contract and must not be mutated at the boundary.
Promise<T> variance lets a caller cast the shared promise; keep the cast in the loader, not at call sites, or a differently-typed consumer breaks the registry's contract.
Delete on settle and bound the registry; a Map keyed by user input grows without limit and pins results until settlement.
Do not pass a caller's AbortSignal into the shared fetch - one caller's abort would cancel everyone; race the wait instead.

variants.name: DataLoader with typed keys
variants.idiom_name: new DataLoader<K, V>(batchFn) with typed per-key load()
variants.implementation_notes: Typed DataLoader: the batch function is (keys: readonly K[]) => Promise<readonly (V | Error)[]>, the loader caches promises per key and batches within a tick, and the per-request instance rule keeps tenant-scoped data apart. Type the key in one place - load(key: K) is the only entry point - so the key type doubles as the coalescing contract, and type the batch result as an element-per-key array so the positional contract is checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: A typed loader instance is still a per-key promise cache: create it per request when users see different data, or tenant scope leaks.
The batch function's return array is positional: return exactly one value or Error per requested key, in order.
load() returns V, not V | Error: rejections must be signalled by returning an Error element (or by rejecting the batch), and the type does not enforce which.
Keys are still stringified or compared by identity at runtime: type the key type accordingly (string or canonicalised) rather than trusting object identity.
